issues.subcategory: Use of simulated/dummy data presented as results
issues.description: The entire Results section, and parts of the Method section, are based on randomly generated dummy data from Qualtrics (N=1000), not actual empirical data. The authors acknowledge this in bracketed notes but then proceed to interpret the results substantively, draw conclusions, and report statistical significance as if the data were real. This renders all reported findings, effect sizes, p-values, and interpretations completely meaningless. The abstract also reports substantive conclusions ('found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis') based on random data.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The Procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which means participants self-selected into experimental conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This fundamentally undermines the between-subjects experimental design and makes causal inference impossible due to self-selection bias. The original study used random assignment.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The original study gave participants actual $5 bills and measured real donation behavior. The replication uses hypothetical/imaginary donation ('indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). This is a major deviation that changes the dependent variable from actual behavior to stated intention, which is known to differ substantially. This undermines the construct validity of the DV and the classification as a 'close to very close replication.'
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original study had participants earn $5 from a prior survey, creating an endowment that they could then donate. The replication removes this entirely ('Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation'). Combined with the switch to hypothetical donation, this removes the key behavioral measure that made the original study meaningful.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: The Design section describes the study as 'a single within-subject design' but the original studies used between-subjects designs, and the rest of the manuscript (including the ANOVA analyses and condition sample sizes in Table 7) clearly treats this as a between-subjects design with different participants in each cell. This is a direct contradiction.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The study is classified as a 'close to very close replication' despite multiple major deviations: (1) hypothetical vs. real donations, (2) online MTurk vs. in-person lab, (3) no endowment/pre-survey compensation, (4) merging two separate studies into one, (5) adding intervention to the joint condition, (6) self-selection into conditions. These collectively represent substantial departures that should classify this as a 'far replication' at best.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: In the text interpreting Table 10, the authors report means for the statistical victim condition (M=2.54, SD=1.76) and identifiable victim condition (M=2.24, SD=1.67), but these values do not match the descriptive statistics in Table 7, which shows identifiable victim means of 2.58 and 2.50 (intervention/no intervention) and statistical victim means of 2.46 and 2.01. The marginal means should be approximately 2.54 for identifiable and 2.24 for statistical, meaning the authors appear to have swapped the condition labels in their interpretation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: Direction of effect contradicts identifiable victim effect
issues.description: The reported finding that statistical victims received MORE donations than identifiable victims directly contradicts the identifiable victim effect (Hypothesis 1 states people donate more to identifiable victims). Yet the authors do not flag this reversal or discuss its implications. If the marginal means are actually swapped (as suggested by Table 7), this is a labeling error; if not, it contradicts the core hypothesis without acknowledgment.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic age range in dummy data
issues.description: The dummy data reports an age range of 18-120 years with a mean of 67.8 and SD of 30.10. An age of 120 is biologically implausible, and the mean age of ~68 is unrealistic for any typical participant sample. While the authors note this is simulated data, presenting these demographics without comment suggests inadequate data validation procedures, and raises concerns about whether similar quality checks will be applied to real data.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males

issues.description: The authors merged Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment and applied the intervention manipulation to the joint condition (which was not done in the original Study 3). This changes the design substantially: the joint condition in the original had no explicit intervention, so adding one creates a condition that never existed in the original study. This makes direct comparison of results problematic and introduces new confounds.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.description: The authors mention excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those who failed attention checks, but provide no details on how many were excluded, what the attention check consisted of, or how prior knowledge was assessed. The final analytic sample size after exclusions is not clearly stated.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Missing power analysis details in main text
issues.description: The power analysis is referenced but only available in supplementary materials. The main text does not report the target sample size, the effect size used for power calculations, the desired power level, or how the N=1000 was determined. This information is essential for evaluating the study design.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.description: The manuscript lacks a Discussion section entirely. There is no interpretation of findings, no comparison with original results in a structured discussion, no consideration of limitations, and no general conclusions. This is a major gap in reporting completeness.

issues.subcategory: Hypothetical vs. real donation as DV
issues.description: Switching from real monetary donation to hypothetical donation fundamentally changes the construct being measured. Hypothetical donation measures stated preference/intention, not actual behavior. The identifiable victim effect may operate differently for hypothetical vs. real decisions due to the absence of real financial consequences, making this a construct validity threat.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children

issues.description: Table 9 reports residual df = 994 for the replication. With N=1000 and a 2×3 design, the residual df should be 1000 - 6 = 994, which is correct. However, the total N across cells in Table 7 sums to 159+175+166+175+159+166 = 1000, yet after exclusions for prior knowledge and attention checks, the actual N should be lower. The dummy data appears to not have applied any exclusion criteria despite stating they would be applied.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The authors state they will only conduct post-hoc contrast tests 'if the interaction effect is significant' and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons 'only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant.' While this is stated in the pre-registration, it introduces analytic flexibility because the decision to conduct follow-up tests depends on initial results, and the criteria for 'significant' are not clearly specified (e.g., alpha level for gating decisions).
issues.quote: Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant

issues.subcategory: Extension hypothesis direction inconsistent with results
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.' However, the significant post-hoc result found was between statistical victims and the joint condition (not identifiable vs. statistical), and it showed statistical victims had HIGHER perceived impact than the joint condition. The hypothesis was not directly supported, yet the abstract claims 'Results have supported the hypothesis.'
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The abstract states 'found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect' but Table 9 shows a significant interaction effect (F=4.25, p=.015). The abstract also claims support for the perceived impact hypothesis, but the actual significant comparison was between statistical and joint conditions, not identifiable vs. statistical as hypothesized.
issues.quote: found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect

issues.description: There is no description of manipulation checks to verify that the intervention (learning about the identifiable victim effect) was effective, or that participants in different identifiability conditions actually perceived the victims differently. The original study's manipulation details are also not fully described.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on aggregated feelings measure
issues.description: The aggregated feelings variable is used in analyses but there is no description of how the individual feeling items were combined (simple average, sum, weighted), what the reliability of the composite was (Cronbach's alpha), or the scale anchors/range for the individual items.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The shift from a controlled laboratory setting (original) to an online MTurk survey introduces numerous potential confounds including reduced attention, environmental distractions, and different participant motivation. This is acknowledged as a deviation but its potential impact on the identifiable victim effect (which may depend on emotional engagement) is not discussed.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: Table 4 ('Difference and similarities between the original study and replication') has three columns but the second and third columns for the replication appear to contain identical information, suggesting a formatting error or that one column was intended for planned vs. actual data collection.
issues.quote: Original study | Qualtrics generated response

issues.subcategory: Effect size confidence intervals include zero despite significance
issues.description: In Table 10, the identifiable vs. statistical comparison is reported as significant (p=.049) but the 95% CI for Cohen's d is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. A significant result at p<.05 should have a 95% CI for the effect size that excludes zero (assuming the CI corresponds to the same test). This inconsistency suggests either a computational error or a mismatch between the test statistic and the effect size CI.

Table 7 shows unequal cell sizes across conditions (ranging from 159 to 175). With random assignment to a 2×3 design and N=1000, approximately equal cell sizes (~167) would be expected. The variation is not explained and could indicate differential attrition or problems with randomization.

The manuscript attributes the identifiable victim effect partly to the 'availability heuristic' (ease of retrieving instances from memory), but the mechanism described is actually closer to the 'affect heuristic' or vividness/imagery effects. The availability heuristic specifically concerns frequency judgments based on ease of recall, not emotional reactions to vivid individual cases.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of original study statistics
issues.description: Multiple cells in Tables 1 and 2 are marked 'N/A' for statistics that should be calculable from the original study (e.g., SDs in Study 3, df2 in Study 3). The error degrees of freedom for Study 3 are missing, making it impossible to verify the reported F-statistics.
issues.quote: Statistical victim | 1.14 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.description: The correlation analysis between aggregated feelings and donation is described as examining 'whether affective feelings predict donation,' implying a causal/predictive relationship. However, correlation does not establish prediction or causation, and both variables are measured simultaneously without temporal precedence or experimental manipulation of feelings.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: Dropped ordered probit regression without justification
issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as one of its analyses, but the replication states 'This test would not be conducted in the replication' without providing any justification for dropping this analysis. This selective omission of an original analytic approach could affect comparability.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication
